notes: Mortgagee sale duty, valuation bracket, and lavender inquiry scope are all clearly resolved in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Mortgagee sale duty and valuation bracket on forced farm sale
key_facts: Mortgagees sold Brellim House Estate by private treaty for £1.625M after repossession, treating extensive lavender plantings as valueless.
The judge found market value of the land alone was £1.75M, that Mr Miller negligently accepted a last-minute £25,000 price reduction, and that expert advice on the lavender was negligent.
The appellants claimed the full £125,000 shortfall and that the estate agent's marketing was negligent; the respondents cross-appealed the scope of an inquiry into separate sale of lavender plants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from a Chancery trial on a mortgagee's duty to obtain the best price reasonably obtainable.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; cross-appeal allowed; inquiry widened to address power and duty to sever and market lavender plants separately.
enrichment.ratio: A mortgagee does not breach his duty simply because the sale price falls within an acceptable bracket of non-negligent valuations, and the bracket approach may assist in assessing whether the mortgagee exercised informed judgment reasonably; however, where no pleaded or fully investigated claim existed as to lifting and selling plants separately, liability findings on that issue should be set aside and the inquiry varied accordingly.
legal_issues: Whether a bracket of non-negligent valuations is relevant to mortgagee breach of duty
Whether the estate agent's marketing and early acceptance of offers were negligent
Whether the judge could order an inquiry on unpleaded lift-and-sell liability for lavender plants

Downsview Nominees Ltd v First City Corporation [1993] AC 295
Yorkshire Bank plc v Hall [1999] 1 WLR 1713
South Australia Asset Management Corp v York Montague Ltd [1997] AC 191

notes: Case-management appeals on Sheffield Supertram litigation; forensic pathway and joinder issues are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Supertram injury claim: appeals restoring council and contractor defendants

statutes_considered.title: South Yorkshire Light Rail Transit Act 1988

key_facts: The claimant suffered serious injuries on 16 May 1995 when his car tyres rode on wet tram rails in Norton Avenue, Sheffield, and he lost control.
Holland J had struck out claims against Balfour Beatty and later entered judgment for Sheffield City Council, leaving the claimant to pursue Supertram companies alone.

The Court of Appeal held the claimant should be permitted to pursue common law and related claims against the council and contractor where documents and skeleton arguments had already developed those cases.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals against case-management decisions restricting the claimant's case to the Supertram promoters.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; orders striking out or dismissing claims against the first and fourth defendants set aside; matter remitted for further case management.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant has a viable common law case against additional defendants and discovery is largely complete, restricting the action to one defendant for case-management economy should not prevent pursuit of other potentially liable parties if that is necessary to achieve the overriding objective and a fair forensic pathway to judgment.
legal_issues: Whether claims against the highway authority and contractor should remain struck out
Whether common law duties arise from the council's design and implementation role
Whether strike-out by reference to inadequately particularised pleadings was premature

Gorringe v Calderdale MBC [2002] RTR 446
Hardaker v Idle District Council [1896] 1 QB 335

notes: Beth Din freezing direction and fraud award; English and Jewish law analysis on charge creation is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Beth Din freezing direction did not charge fraudster's sold home
key_facts: Orthodox Jewish parties referred a fraud dispute to a Beth Din, which granted an interlocutory direction restraining sale of Mr Jason's Hendon home and later awarded £237,224.50 damages.
Mr Jason breached the direction, sold the property to Mr and Mrs Sherman, emigrated, and accepted a reduced personal settlement.
Mr Kastner sought to enforce a charging order against the property; the purchasers argued they took free of any lien.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Concurrent Chancery trials on whether Beth Din orders created a proprietary charge binding purchasers.
enrichment.outcome: Purchasers entitled to registration free of charge; interim charging order discharged; no final charging order.
enrichment.ratio: A Beth Din freezing direction and caution, like an English freezing order, does not create a charge over land; under Jewish law no retrospective charge bound purchasers who completed before the Beth Din quantified liability, and absent an award declaring such a charge the English court would not impose one on non-parties.
legal_issues: Whether the Beth Din had jurisdiction to grant the freezing direction
Whether the direction, caution, or award created a charge or lien
Whether Jewish law on fraudsters' property binds English purchasers
linked_authorities: Flightline Ltd v Edwards [2003] 1 WLR 1200
Elias v Mitchell [1972] Ch 652

confidence.notes: Detailed findings on jurisdiction and absence of proprietary security are explicit.

notes: Police injury-on-duty pension appeal applying Stunt; reasoning closely follows Court of Appeal authority.

enrichment.short_title: Police witness absence publicity not an injury on duty
key_facts: PC Knapper missed a criminal trial while on holiday in Tenerife, attracting adverse judicial and press comment and subsequent mental illness ending his service.
He retired on ill-health pension and sought an additional injury-on-duty award.
Medical referee Dr Watt allowed the appeal, treating the psychiatric injury as caused because he would not have suffered it had he not been known to be a constable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a medical referee's decision under the Police Pensions Regulations 1987.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed; Dr Watt's decision quashed.
enrichment.ratio: Psychiatric injury arising from adverse publicity after a police officer failed to attend court as a witness is not an injury received in the execution of duty under regulation A11; it falls on the wrong side of R (Stunt) v Mallett and cannot be saved by regulation A11(2)(b).
legal_issues: Meaning of injury received in the execution of duty
Application of regulation A11(2)(b)
Whether Stunt distinguishes disciplinary stress from witness-absence publicity
linked_authorities: R (Stunt) v Mallett [2001] ICR 989
R v Kellam ex parte South Wales Police Authority [2000] ICR 632

confidence.notes: Central issue is governed by Stunt and applied straightforwardly.

notes: Short planning appeal on s294 Crown immunity wording; statutory construction is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Crown planning immunity under section 294 requires Crown land
key_facts: During the 2001 foot-and-mouth outbreak DEFRA carried out large-scale engineering works at Westlake Farm under licence from private owners Mr and Mrs Stevens.
Mid-Devon District Council served enforcement notices; an inspector quashed them on the basis that Crown development immunity applied even though the land was never Crown land.
The site was never used as a carcass disposal facility and restoration terms remained disputed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 appeal against an enforcement-notice appeal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; inspector's decision quashed and remitted for rehearing on remaining grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Section 294(1) of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 confers immunity from enforcement only where development was carried out by or on behalf of the Crown on land that was Crown land at the time of the development; private owners cannot rely on Crown immunity for development on their own land merely because Crown contractors performed the works.
legal_issues: Construction of section 294(1)
Whether Crown development immunity attaches to the development or only Crown land
Effect of Lord Advocate v Dumbarton District Council
linked_authorities: Lord Advocate v Dumbarton District Council [1990] 2 AC 580
British Broadcasting Corporation v Johns [1965] Ch 32

notes: Section 172 signature requirement; authority chain from Boss v Measures to Broomfield is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Section 172 driver form must be signed to identify driver
key_facts: A Jaguar registered to the appellant was recorded speeding at 41 mph in a 30 mph zone.
He returned the section 172 form with his details and driver number in Part 1 but left the signature blank.
Magistrates convicted him of failing to provide required driver information; he appealed by case stated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from magistrates' conviction under section 172(3).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; magistrates were correct to convict.
enrichment.ratio: Section 172(2) empowers a chief officer of police to require reasonable information in a reasonable manner, including a signed written response; an unsigned Part 1 form does not identify the driver and section 12(1) presupposes a signed statement for use as evidence of identity.
legal_issues: Whether a signature is required under section 172(2)
Interaction between section 172 and section 12 RTOA 1988
Whether PACE Code C required a caution

notes: Large tobacco RICO letter-of-request appeal; privilege analysis is extensive but outcome is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Tobacco RICO letter of request: Foyle examination ordered
key_facts: The United States sought examination of Lovells partner Andrew Foyle about BAT group's document management and destruction policies in massive RICO proceedings.
BATCo intervened claiming blanket legal advice and litigation privilege over nine years of communications.
Moore-Bick J ordered examination subject to phased privilege rulings; BATCo and Mr Foyle appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Commercial Court order for examination pursuant to US letters of request.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; examination to proceed with judicial control over privilege objections.
enrichment.ratio: Legal advice privilege is not blanket where a solicitor's retainer mixed legal advice with non-legal document-management tasks, and litigation privilege did not attach from 1985-86 because litigation against BATCo was not reasonably in prospect; the court should assist letters of request unless it is clear at the outset that substantive questions will be blocked by privilege.
legal_issues: Scope of legal advice privilege after Three Rivers (No 5) and (No 10)
Whether litigation was reasonably in prospect for BATCo
Whether examination would be oppressive
Fair balance between requesting court and witness interests

notes: Home Detention Curfew unlawfully-at-large calculation; statutory scheme and absurdity examples are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Unlawfully at large during HDC shifts entire sentence dates
key_facts: Mr Lindo was sentenced to two years, released on Home Detention Curfew 87 days before the halfway point, had HDC revoked on 7 April 2003, and was unlawfully at large for 17 days.
He argued only the automatic conditional release date should move back 17 days, not licence expiry or sentence expiry.
The Secretary of State recalculated licence expiry to account for the 17-day absence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review appeal on computation of release and licence dates after HDC recall.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Secretary of State's calculation upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 49(2) of the Prison Act 1952, time unlawfully at large after HDC revocation is not counted toward detention and effectively freezes the sentence, shifting all subsequent release dates including licence expiry and sentence expiry by the same period.
legal_issues: Effect of section 49(2) after section 38A(5) unlawfully-at-large status
Whether HDC and ordinary licence regimes differ on date calculation
Whether the appellant suffers double penalisation
linked_authorities: R (S) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 426

notes: Planning sustainability reasoning quashed for inadequacy; PPG3 paragraph 70 analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Coldwaltham housing appeal quashed for inadequate sustainability reasons
key_facts: An inspector granted planning permission for 18 dwellings at Coldwaltham, West Sussex, despite highway authority objections on transport sustainability.
The council argued the village was remote, poorly served by buses, and not a suitable location under PPG3 paragraph 70.
The inspector accepted sustainability concerns but held supporting local services outweighed them and reduced parking from 2 to 1.5 spaces per dwelling.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to a planning inspector's decision after informal appeal hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Where sustainability was a main issue, the inspector failed to give intelligible reasons for concluding the development would support local services and did not properly apply PPG3 paragraph 70 or address why reduced parking cured an unsustainable remote location with inadequate public transport.
legal_issues: Adequacy of inspector's reasons on sustainability
Application of PPG3 paragraph 70 to village infill
Whether reducing car parking standards addressed transport objections

confidence.notes: Quashing decision rests on established inadequate-reasons grounds with detailed paragraph-by-paragraph analysis.

notes: Interlocutory patent decision on collateral use of compelled evidence; EPO rejection and partial release make downstream use uncertain.

enrichment.short_title: Patent prior-use evidence: limited collateral use permitted abroad
key_facts: Dendron sought revocation of EP 0 803 230 concerning apparatus for deploying Guglielmi Detachable Coils to treat aneurysms.
Dendron alleged extensive public prior use before the priority date and obtained letters of request for witnesses in Germany and Alabama plus US section 1782 evidence.
The defendants disclosed confidential patient-related material under a confidentiality club and opposed wider use in EPO, Dutch, and German proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory Patents Court application on collateral use of compelled evidence and disclosure.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused for EPO use; permission granted for German and Dutch proceedings in respect of Schumacher and Horton testimony; English disclosure collateral use refused.
enrichment.ratio: Evidence obtained under compulsion carries an implied restriction on collateral use; release is justified only where it serves justice and the foreign tribunal will receive the material, but anonymised prior-use evidence from neutral professionals may be released for parallel foreign validity proceedings where no injustice is shown.
legal_issues: Whether Regulation 1206/2001 or common law restricts collateral use of letter-of-request evidence
Exercise of discretion under SmithKline Beecham principles
Whether EPO would admit late prior-use evidence
